title: Las Animas Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Las Animas wells have a 60-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $8,100-$15,300.
intro_html:
Las Animas sits on the plains, where well records show mostly shallow water supplies in alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. The local permit file includes domestic, stock, irrigation and monitoring wells, but the records do not tell the whole story for every property.

For a buyer, the useful questions are practical: how deep might the hole be, what flow rate is realistic, and what should a complete water system cost? Neighboring permits near the lot, local geology, and a proper site review matter more than a countywide average alone.

sections.heading: Las Animas well depths reflect shallow plains geology
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Las Animas is 60 feet. The middle half runs from 33 to 240 feet, so nearby wells can vary substantially even across the same general area. A deeper record reaches 545 feet, while 59% of wells are under 100 feet.

Another 20% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and 20% are between 300 and 600 feet. That spread matters when reviewing a drilling bid. A 60-foot estimate may fit one parcel but not another, particularly where the alluvial section is thin or the driller must continue into sedimentary rock. Check permits closest to the property before relying on the median.

sections.heading: What Las Animas wells produce
sections.html:
Only 87 permitted wells report a pump yield, so the yield statistics are more limited than the depth records. Among those reports, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 30.0 gallons per minute.

The reported results are generally favorable: 51% produce more than 15 gallons per minute, and 46% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Another 3% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, while 0% are under 1 gallon per minute in this dataset. A buyer should still confirm the permitted use, storage needs, and a new well's actual pump test rather than treating the median as a guarantee.

sections.heading: The Las Animas water table appears shallow
sections.html:
Just 12 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is small. Those records show a median depth to water of 14 feet, with the middle half from 8 to 40 feet. That supports the picture of shallow groundwater in at least part of the local plains setting.

The available facts do not provide a water-level series by decade, so they do not establish a reliable long-term rise or decline. Static water level is also not the same as the pumping level while a well is operating. Before buying, ask for the well permit, completion report, current pump performance and any recent water-level information for the specific property.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long local drilling activity
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records list 817 permitted wells within the mapped area around Las Animas. Of those, 596 are recorded as constructed and 607 report a total depth. Permits appear from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025.

Activity was highest in the 2000s, with 168 permits, followed by the 1990s with 129. The records identify Hoffman, Earl with 82 wells, Authorized, Pe, Pg with 63, and Crandall, H A with 31. Those names describe recorded permit history, not a recommendation or proof that a driller is currently available.

sections.heading: A Las Animas well budget starts with depth
sections.html:
For the alluvium and plains sedimentary rock around Las Animas, the drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the local median depth of 60 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $2,100-$3,300. That is only the borehole portion, not the complete water system.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $8,100-$15,300 at that median depth. Deeper ground, casing, grout, difficult access, longer trenching and electrical work can change the bid. Get the driller to separate drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, testing, trenching and power so competing estimates can be compared accurately.

sections.heading: Checks for water quality, yield and building plans
sections.html:
The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 4 historic mine features and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Their presence does not prove a particular parcel is contaminated, but it is a reason to review environmental records and test the well water before closing.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible even where nearby wells perform well. Confirm the well location, permitted use and completion details with Colorado DWR. Septic setbacks, access for a drill rig, casing and grout requirements, and the route for water and power should be evaluated before finalizing a homesite. Domestic wells are generally limited to household uses under their permit, not unrestricted irrigation.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Las Animas
sections.html:
Start with the closest neighboring permits, not only the countywide numbers. Compare depths, aquifers, reported yields and construction dates for the lot and nearby areas such as Hasty, Cheraw, North La Junta, La Junta Gardens, La Junta and McClave. Local records identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers in 683 wells, Dakota in 54, and Cheyenne in 39; no Denver Basin aquifer wells are recorded.

Before purchasing, make the contract contingent on reviewing the permit and testing the existing system, if there is one. For a vacant lot, obtain a site-specific drilling opinion and a complete water-system estimate. Also confirm septic feasibility, driveway access, electrical service and the intended household or stock use before designing the home.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Las Animas, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Las Animas is 60 feet. The middle half runs from 33 to 240 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 545 feet. About 59% are under 100 feet, but local conditions vary, so nearby permits are more useful for estimating a specific parcel than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Las Animas?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 60-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,100-$3,300. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $8,100-$15,300. Deeper drilling, access, casing, grout and utility work can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Las Animas?
faq.a: Among the 87 wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0-30.0 gallons per minute. The records show 51% above 15 gallons per minute and 3% between 1 and 5. These figures are not a guarantee for a new well or a particular property.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Las Animas?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that every well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, the mapped area includes 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 4 historic mine features and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test an existing or new well for relevant contaminants and review nearby environmental records before relying on it for household water.

faq.q: What aquifers do Las Animas wells use?
faq.a: The largest recorded group is unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with 683 wells. Dakota aquifer wells account for 54, and Cheyenne wells account for 39. No Denver Basin aquifer wells are recorded. These labels come from permits and should be compared with the specific property's completion report and nearby well records.
